name: Perilla seed extract

lead: Perilla seed extract comes from Perilla frutescens, a mint-family herb used in Korean, Chinese, Japanese and Indian cooking; the seeds are roughly 38 to 45 percent oil. It appears in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 and antioxidant ingredient, used for softer, smoother, more comfortable skin.

The chain is barrier support: the plant oils soften the skin surface, and the extract and its component luteolin reduced inflammatory signalling in animal and cell studies. Published work is limited to laboratory and animal studies; human appearance trials were not found.

paras: Used in creams, oils and serums as a botanical emollient step after cleansing, often layered with other moisturising ingredients. Users typically describe softer skin soon after application and a gradual improvement in comfort and smoothness over weeks.
Perilla seed allergy, including anaphylaxis, is documented in children and adults, and contact dermatitis can occur from handling. People with seed allergies commonly avoid it.

angle.text: Perilla seed extract is included in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 and antioxidant ingredient, used for softer, smoother skin. The oil-rich seed softens the skin surface, and the extract reduced inflammatory signalling in animal and cell studies.

lead: Perilla seed extract is derived from the seeds of Perilla frutescens, a mint-family annual used in Korean, Chinese, Japanese and Indian cooking; the seeds contain roughly 38 to 45 percent oil.[1] It appears in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 or antioxidant ingredient, which brands position as a way to condition skin and support a healthy-looking complexion, and a 2025 laboratory study has also examined seed extracts for hair-loss-related pathways.[2]

Published work consists mainly of laboratory and animal studies, including anti-inflammatory effects in mouse colitis models, antioxidant and immune-cell studies in cultured cells, and an in vitro hair-loss study.[3][2][4][5] The extract's main characterised phytochemicals include rosmarinic acid and luteolin.[5] Perilla seed allergy is documented in children, and handling can cause contact dermatitis.[1][6] No clinical study of perilla seed extract for skin appearance was found.

paras: Perilla frutescens, called deulkkae in Korea and egoma in Japan, is an annual of the mint family. Its seeds contain about 38 to 45 percent lipid, and extracts range from pressed oil to solvent or supercritical-fluid preparations.[1][2] Extracts examined in research are rich in polyphenols: a Thai study of 'Nga-Kee-Mon' seed extract reported high total phenolic and flavonoid content and identified rosmarinic acid and luteolin as major phytochemicals.[5]

Perilla seeds and their oil are culinary ingredients in Korea, where toasted seed powder and oil season dishes such as soups and kimchi, and in Japan, where egoma seed paste is used on grilled rice patties. In India roasted seeds are ground into chutney, and the plant is also used in traditional medicine in parts of Southeast Asia.[1] Animal-feed research has tested seed extract in lambs for rumen fermentation and meat quality.[7] Chemistry research has also tested the extract as a corrosion inhibitor, where luteolin and apigenin were identified as the active components.[8]

A 2025 mouse study reported that perilla seed extract and its component luteolin reduced inflammation in an inflammatory bowel disease model: 32 mice were split into four groups and the extract group showed greater villus-to-crypt ratio and goblet cell density than the group given the inflammatory challenge alone, with changes in inflammatory markers reported to involve the PI3K/AKT pathway.[3] A 2024 study in mice with chemically induced ulcerative colitis found that rosmarinic-acid-enriched seed meal and seed extracts at 50 to 500 mg/kg attenuated colonic pathology and lowered proinflammatory cytokines.[4]

The Thai study characterised antioxidant capacity and reported that the extract caused apoptosis in a human colon cancer cell line and reduced secretion of IL-1 beta, IL-6 and TNF-alpha from stimulated mouse macrophage cells.[5] A 2025 in vitro study compared maceration, screw pressing and supercritical fluid extraction of perilla seed and examined effects on androgenetic-alopecia-related pathways, with the supercritical extract containing the highest polyunsaturated fatty acid levels.[2] Another 2025 study tested ginsenosides and perilla seed extracts on liver-cell lipid and glucose handling.[9] These are not human appearance trials.

Eating large quantities of seeds has caused anaphylaxis, and handling leaves or oil may cause contact dermatitis.[1] A study of 21 children with perilla seed allergy reported a median age of 3 years, anaphylaxis in 28.6 percent, a positive prick test in all 15 children tested, and positive specific IgE in 85.7 percent, and noted there was no established diagnostic test before it developed one.[6] The plant is also toxic to cattle and horses through perilla ketone, which causes respiratory distress in grazing animals.[1]
No studies found on perilla seed extract for skin or appearance. Human data are limited to allergy case series.[6]
